rows.stem: If \(A = [a_{ij}]\) is a square matrix of order 2 such that \(a_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{when } i \ne j \\ 0, & \text{when } i = j \end{cases}\), then \(A^2\) is
rows.solution: The two conditions fix every entry of the \(2 \times 2\) matrix: the diagonal entries have \(i = j\) so \(a_{11} = a_{22} = 0\), and the off-diagonal entries have \(i \ne j\) so \(a_{12} = a_{21} = 1\). Hence \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Squaring, \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 & 0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0 \\ 1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 & 1 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). So \(A^2\) is the identity matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

rows.stem: The value of the determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} 6 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix}\) is
rows.solution: Expand along the first row, where the zero in the middle position kills one term: \(\begin{vmatrix} 6 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 6(1 \times 3 - 4 \times 1) - 0(2 \times 3 - 4 \times 1) + (-1)(2 \times 1 - 1 \times 1)\). This is \(6(3 - 4) - 0 + (-1)(2 - 1) = -6 - 1 = -7\), so the value of the determinant is \(-7\).

rows.stem: The function \(f(x) = x\,|\,x\,|\), \(x \in R\) is differentiable
rows.solution: Write the modulus piecewise: \(f(x) = x^2\) for \(x \ge 0\) and \(f(x) = -x^2\) for \(x < 0\). Each piece is a polynomial, so \(f\) is certainly differentiable at every \(x \ne 0\); only the join needs checking. There \(f(0) = 0\), and the right-hand derivative is \(\lim_{h \to 0^+} \dfrac{f(0 + h) - f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \dfrac{h^2}{h} = 0\), while the left-hand derivative is \(\lim_{h \to 0^-} \dfrac{f(0 + h) - f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \dfrac{-h^2}{h} = 0\). The two agree, so \(f'(0) = 0\) exists. Hence \(f\) is differentiable at every real number, i.e. in R, with \(f'(x) = 2|x|\).

rows.subtopic: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem
rows.solution: An antiderivative of \(\sin 2x\) is \(-\dfrac{\cos 2x}{2}\), so \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \sin 2x\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{\cos 2x}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = -\dfrac{\cos(\pi/2)}{2} + \dfrac{\cos 0}{2} = -0 + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). So the value is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

rows.stem: A unit vector \(\hat{a}\) makes equal but acute angles on the co-ordinate axes. The projection of the vector \(\hat{a}\) on the vector \(\vec{b} = 5\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} - \hat{k}\) is
rows.solution: Equal angles with the three axes make the direction cosines of \(\hat{a}\) equal, and the angles being acute makes them positive. So \(l = m = n > 0\) with \(l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1\), giving \(l = m = n = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(\hat{a} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})\). Now \(|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 7^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}\) and \(\hat{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(5 + 7 - 1) = \dfrac{11}{\sqrt{3}}\). Hence the projection of \(\hat{a}\) on \(\vec{b}\) is \(\dfrac{\hat{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = \dfrac{11/\sqrt{3}}{5\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{11}{5 \times 3} = \dfrac{11}{15}\).

rows.stem: If A and B are two independent events such that \(P(A) = \dfrac{1}{3}\) and \(P(B) = \dfrac{1}{4}\), then \(P(B'/A)\) is
rows.solution: By definition \(P(B'/A) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B')}{P(A)}\). Since \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, so are \(A\) and \(B'\), giving \(P(A \cap B') = P(A)\,P(B')\). Hence \(P(B'/A) = \dfrac{P(A)\,P(B')}{P(A)} = P(B') = 1 - P(B) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}\). Note that \(P(A) = \dfrac{1}{3}\) is not needed at all: under independence, conditioning on the event A changes nothing. So the required probability is \(\dfrac{3}{4}\).

rows.subtopic: Domains, Ranges and Principal Value Branches
rows.stem: Draw the graph of the principal branch of the function \(f(x) = \cos^{-1} x\).
rows.solution: The principal branch of \(f(x) = \cos^{-1} x\) has domain \([-1, 1]\) and range \([0, \pi]\), and its graph is the reflection of \(y = \cos x\), \(x \in [0, \pi]\), in the line \(y = x\). To draw it, mark the three anchor points \((-1, \pi)\), \(\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and \((1, 0)\) and join them by a single smooth falling arc. The fall is strict because \(f'(x) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} < 0\) on \((-1, 1)\), and the same expression shows the tangent becomes vertical as \(x \to -1^+\) and \(x \to 1^-\), so the arc meets the two end points steeply. Since \(f''(x) = -\dfrac{x}{(1 - x^2)^{3/2}}\) changes sign at \(x = 0\), the arc is concave up on \((-1, 0)\) and concave down on \((0, 1)\), with its point of inflection at \(\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Nothing is drawn outside \(-1 \le x \le 1\), and the curve never leaves the strip \(0 \le y \le \pi\).

The angle between two lines depends only on their direction vectors, here \(\vec{b_1} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{b_2} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\). If \(\theta\) is the angle between the lines, then \(\cos\theta = \left|\dfrac{\vec{b_1} \cdot \vec{b_2}}{|\vec{b_1}|\,|\vec{b_2}|}\right|\). Here \(\vec{b_1} \cdot \vec{b_2} = 3 + 4 + 12 = 19\), \(|\vec{b_1}| = \sqrt{9 + 4 + 36} = 7\) and \(|\vec{b_2}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3\). Hence \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{19}{7 \times 3} = \dfrac{19}{21}\), so \(\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{19}{21}\right)\).

rows.stem: Using determinants, find the area of \(\Delta PQR\) with vertices P(3, 1), Q(9, 3) and R(5, 7). Also, find the equation of line PQ using determinants.
rows.solution: Area of \(\Delta PQR = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 9 & 3 & 1 \\ 5 & 7 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\right|\). Expanding along the first row, the determinant is \(3(3 \times 1 - 1 \times 7) - 1(9 \times 1 - 1 \times 5) + 1(9 \times 7 - 3 \times 5) = 3(-4) - 1(4) + 1(48) = -12 - 4 + 48 = 32\). Hence the area is \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 32 = 16\) square units. For line PQ, a point \((x, y)\) lies on it exactly when \((x, y)\), P(3, 1) and Q(9, 3) are collinear, i.e. \(\begin{vmatrix} x & y & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 9 & 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Expanding along the first row, \(x(1 - 3) - y(3 - 9) + (9 - 9) = 0\), that is \(-2x + 6y = 0\), which on dividing by \(-2\) becomes \(x - 3y = 0\). Both P and Q satisfy it, as they must.

Let \(I = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\cos 2x}{1 + \cos 2x}\,dx\). Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) leaves the integrand unchanged, so it is even and \(I = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\cos 2x}{1 + \cos 2x}\,dx\). Now split off the constant part: \(\dfrac{\cos 2x}{1 + \cos 2x} = \dfrac{(1 + \cos 2x) - 1}{1 + \cos 2x} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + \cos 2x}\), and since \(1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x\) this is \(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2 x\). Hence \(I = 2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\sec^2 x\right)dx = 2\left[x - \dfrac{1}{2}\tan x\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \left[2x - \tan x\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}\). At the upper limit this is \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1\) and at the lower limit it is \(0\), so \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1\).

Let \(I = \displaystyle\int e^{x^2}(x^5 + 2x^3)\,dx\) and put \(x^2 = t\), so that \(2x\,dx = dt\). Pulling one factor of \(x\) out to meet \(dx\), \((x^5 + 2x^3)\,dx = (x^4 + 2x^2)\,x\,dx = (t^2 + 2t)\dfrac{dt}{2}\), and therefore \(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int e^{t}(t^2 + 2t)\,dt\). The bracket is exactly of the form \(f(t) + f'(t)\) with \(f(t) = t^2\), and \(\displaystyle\int e^{t}\{f(t) + f'(t)\}\,dt = e^{t}f(t) + C\). Hence \(I = \dfrac{1}{2}e^{t}t^2 + C = \dfrac{1}{2}x^4 e^{x^2} + C\). Checking by differentiation, \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x^4 e^{x^2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(4x^3 e^{x^2} + x^4 \cdot 2x\,e^{x^2}\right) = e^{x^2}(2x^3 + x^5)\), which is the original integrand.

rows.subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
rows.stem: Find the area of the minor segment of the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 4\) cut off by the line \(x = 1\), using integration.
rows.solution: The circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 4\) has centre at the origin and radius \(2\), and the line \(x = 1\) meets it where \(y^2 = 3\), i.e. at \((1, \sqrt{3})\) and \((1, -\sqrt{3})\). The minor segment is the smaller of the two pieces the chord cuts off, so it is the region to the RIGHT of \(x = 1\), bounded by the chord and the arc, running from \(x = 1\) to \(x = 2\). It is symmetric about the x-axis, so Area \(= 2\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\sqrt{4 - x^2}\,dx\). Using \(\displaystyle\int\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx = \dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \dfrac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{a}\) with \(a = 2\), Area \(= 2\left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{4 - x^2} + 2\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{2}\right]_{1}^{2}\). At \(x = 2\) the bracket is \(0 + 2\sin^{-1}(1) = 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \pi\); at \(x = 1\) it is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{3} + 2\sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Hence Area \(= 2\left(\pi - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}\) square units, about \(2.46\). As a check, the chord subtends a central angle of \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\), and the standard formula \(\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\phi - \sin\phi)\) gives the same value.

[CBSE marking scheme: the penultimate line is printed as \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\left[\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - \tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]\), a bracket whose two terms are identical and which therefore evaluates to \(0\), not to the \(\pi\) printed on the very next line. The lower limit \(x = 0\) contributes \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), so the bracket should read \(\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = -1 - 1 = -2\). Only that one line is mistyped; the scheme's method and its final answer \(\pi\) are correct.] Let \(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{x}{1 + \sin x}\,dx\). Apply \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}f(a - x)\,dx\) with \(a = \pi\); since \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\), this gives \(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{\pi - x}{1 + \sin x}\,dx\). Adding the two expressions for \(I\), the \(x\) terms cancel and \(2I = \pi\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{dx}{1 + \sin x}\), so \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{dx}{1 + \sin x}\). Now \(1 + \sin x = 1 + \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = 2\cos^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\), hence \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\sec^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)dx = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left[-2\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right]_{0}^{\pi}\). Evaluating, \(I = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\left[\tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}(-1 - 1) = \pi\). As an independent check, \(t = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}\) turns \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\dfrac{dx}{1 + \sin x}\) into \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{2\,dt}{(1 + t)^2} = 2\), giving \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \times 2 = \pi\).
